articles.title: Xbox to limit cloud gaming to 15 hours a month for Game Pass users
articles.summary: Xbox said the limits were due to the rising cost of cloud gaming, and would allow it to invest more in its performance
articles.body:
Xbox is introducing strict monthly time limits for Game Pass subscribers who stream games online through its cloud gaming service.

The changes, which come into effect in November, will see a subscriber to the £16.99 Ultimate monthly plan able to stream games for up to 15 hours a month - before having to purchase additional cloud play time.

Xbox said the limits were due to the rising cost of cloud gaming, and they would allow the firm to "continue to invest" in the service's "reliability and performance".

While some questioned whether the service was used by many to begin with, others called out the additional limits for subscribers.

Cloud gaming allows players to stream and play games online from a remote server using a phone, tablet or controller, rather than downloading and running it on a PC or console at home.

Different tiers of subscription to Game Pass will have different limits.

Premium users will get 10 hours, while those on the basic Essential tier will get five hours a month before they have to pay for extra time.

Xbox claimed just 4% of the people who use Games Pass - its Netflix-style subscription plan for games - use its cloud gaming service.

A recent Wall Street Journal article reported Game Pass has 30 million subscribers, which would leave the number of people affected by the cloud gaming changes at roughly 1.2 million.

"This is a pretty awful change, hopefully Xbox adds an extra zero on the end cause 15hrs is abysmal. 30 minutes a day, really?" posted one commenter on X .

Jez Corden of Windows Central told the BBC the announcement showed that "absolutely nothing is safe from the AI-driven component crisis," but he added it also highlighted "where Microsoft's priorities are".

Both cloud gaming and AI use data centres to process information.

"For them to continue to offer unlimited access to Microsoft Copilot [AI] for free but restrict paid cloud gaming in this way shows some contradiction," he added.

Xbox said in a blog post that from November, users would also be able to use the company's cloud gaming feature without subscribing to Game Pass, but by buying "cloud playtime hours" through the Xbox store.

It has not revealed how much extra hours of cloud gaming would cost.

The news comes as Asha Sharma, Xbox's chief executive, told the BBC in an exclusive recent interview that the company and the industry as a whole needed to "start to innovate on affordability and efficiency," amid a "crisis" in computing prices.

"As an industry, we're in the middle of 'Rampocalypse'. We're in the middle of people coming back from Covid and the patterns changing," she said.

"Rampocalypse" refers to the fact that the cost of a previously cheap hardware component, random access memory (Ram), has shot up in price with the expansion of compute-hungry data centres. Some people also call it "Ramageddon" .

Sharma added: "Within Xbox, we haven't been healthy. And so a lot of the reset that will take us throughout the year is really meant to help ensure that we are here for the next 25 years and we're continuing to serve our purpose and our mission."

According to Xbox owner Microsoft's July financial filings , annual Xbox revenue dropped by $1.7bn to roughly $21.8bn (£16.1bn) - a 7% decline from 2025.

Part of Sharma's reset has seen 3,200 people let go at the company - with 1,600 job losses announced in July, and the remaining posts to go gradually over the course of Microsoft's 2027 financial year.

Studios which had been acquired by Xbox - including Compulsion Games, which made the Bafta-winning South of Midnight and Double Fine Productions, makers of Psychonauts - were also made independent again.

Sharma is betting these changes can reverse its fortunes despite concerns over its subscription strategy and rising AI-related costs.

"Sometimes you have to restructure a business when it's not doing well, and that was true with our Xbox business," Microsoft's president Brad Smith recently told the BBC.

In an interview in July, Jeff Gattiss, Amazon's head of gaming, told the BBC he believed the rising cost of tech would mean people will turn to streaming games online rather than buying new consoles.

However, despite some big names investing in the technology, it has never fully reached the mainstream.

Google launched its own cloud gaming service Stadia in November 2019, positioning it as a "Netflix for games".

The service was discontinued in January 2023 after the company said it had not attracted as many users as hoped.

For many gamers, cloud gaming remains too unreliable for regular use due to its reliance on high-speed internet - and an additional fee may further limit its appeal.

articles.title: Wolverine Legend Hugh Jackman Looks Set to Invest in an English Football Team, Following Deadpool Star Ryan Reynolds' Success With Wrexham
articles.summary: Hugh Jackman's Wolverine looks set to follow Ryan Reynolds' Deadpool in co-owning an English football team.
articles.body:
Hugh Jackman's Wolverine looks set to follow Ryan Reynolds' Deadpool in co-owning an English football team.

Jackman has long been a fan of Norwich City F.C., a second-tier squad from the east of England nicknamed the Canaries, which has spent the last few decades continually on the bubble of achieving top-level success.

Speaking to TalkSport , Jackman mentioned he began supporting Norwich as a child due to it being the birthplace of his mother. And despite growing up in Australia, Jackman has still made various trips to Norwich's home ground over the years. Major cup and league success have proved elusive for Norwich over this time, however, with every successful promotion to the Premier League typically followed by swift relegation the season after.

Marvel's Wolverine: Every Costume in the PS5 Game

"It's been slim pickings," Jackman admitted of Norwich's success rate over the past four decades. "We did win the Milk Cup in 1984. It's not even called the Milk Cup anymore. But we're on the rise. We're on the up and up.

"I went to Carrow Road a couple of times and love the Canaries, and this is the year," he stated. "We're going to get promoted. This is my prediction, Norwich and Wrexham are getting promoted this year."

@talksport Hugh Jackman reveals why he supports Norwich City! 💛💚 The Death of Robin Hood is in cinemas now. #ncfc #norwichcity #norwich #hughjackman ♬ original sound - talkSPORT

Hugh Jackman reveals why he supports Norwich City! 💛💚 The Death of Robin Hood is in cinemas now. #ncfc #norwichcity #norwich #hughjackman

So, could Jackman follow in the footsteps of his Deadpool & Wolverine co-star Ryan Reynolds, who has famously helped shepherd Wrexham FC to success? Asked for a response to rumors he was preparing to buy a significant stake in the club, Jackman grinned and responded:

"I'm very, very interested... and talking about it right now."

Here's hoping the Canaries get powered up with some Adamantium claws.

Tom Phillips is IGN's News Editor. You can reach Tom at tom_phillips@ign.com or find him on Bluesky @tomphillipseg.bsky.social

articles.title: Lego Skylines Hands-On Preview: It’s a Cozy, More Relaxing City-Builder
articles.summary: If you’re like me and looking for something a little less… punishing, shall we say, Lego Skylines might fit the bill. The developers described it to me as a cozier, simpler city builder. You’ll still have problems – crime, fires, you know, the things cities deal with – but you’ll have time to solve them.
articles.body:
You don’t build with individual bricks; instead, you assemble your city with pre-fabricated buildings however you see fit.

It’s cozy and chill, but not entirely so, as your citizens will still present you problems that need solving.

There are plenty of deeper gameplay systems to dig into if you want to.

I love Legos. When I was a kid, my parents would always buy me a set or two for Christmas, and we’d spend part of the day putting it together forever. It was always the more outlandish stuff: pirates and castles and Aquasharks over real-life things, but I did have this pizza delivery truck I adored. This was before Legos largely became all about licensed properties, but the freedom to build whatever you want, however you want, has never really left.

Lego Skylines is all about that, and after spending about an hour with it at Gamescom, I’m excited to play more of it. My demo started simply enough: I was a Master Builder who had come to a little island and run into a family that needed a new house. Since this is a video game, their problems were my problems, and I built them a house. But you know what they say about giving a minifigure a house. Well, they’ll want more. Soon I was sprucing up their yard, building a road, and a place for them to work. And after that, I was on my way to building a whole city.

Let me be clear: this isn’t a brick-by-brick thing. I’m choosing from pre-built houses and buildings (and there are several varieties of each) and watching them come together, piece by piece, at incredible speed. But the cool thing, according to the developers at Iceflake Studios, is that every building in Lego Skylines is built from real Lego bricks in real configurations, and you can see them if you decide, for whatever reason, to demolish something you’ve built. If you have the right pieces, you could build everything in Skylines yourself. That’s awesome.

For me, city builders are more about making a beautiful pattern than making a city that works. Generally, I make my city and then worry about making it a place that functions. As you can imagine, that sometimes gets me into trouble. If you’re like me and looking for something a little less… punishing, shall we say, Lego Skylines might fit the bill. The developers described it to me as a cozier, simpler city builder. You’ll still have problems – crime, fires, you know, the things cities deal with – but you’ll have time to solve them. This isn’t a situation where things will start collapsing immediately if you don’t take care of them. There won’t be Lego minifigures roaming the streets with pitchforks and torches because they don’t have healthcare.

What that means is you can kind of build your city how you want to. One of the developers I spoke to told me she focuses on building a cozy city until problems start piling up. Another told me he starts with taking care of what needs to happen first and foremost and then worries about making it pretty afterwards. Whatever you want to do is fine.

What I really appreciated, though, was just how many options I had and how complex things could get if I really wanted to dig. If I wanted to attract people, I needed jobs, which meant places for them to work, which meant roads to take them there. And if I wanted people to visit those fine establishments, I had to advertise them (billboards!) and make them more appealing (Statues! Flowers! Fountains!). The same was true of any house, too, and I could always click on a resident or building and figure out what issues needed solving or if they were happy with things the way they were.

After I spent a while building up my own town, I played the second part of the demo, which took me to a finished city, and man, it was impressive in a “how on Earth would you build this?” sort of way. But that’s the thing, right? Building a city is a process, and like real cities, they change all the time. You might move a building, add a road, add a park. Stores go up and come down. Cities and towns are living things that grow and change and shrink and decay and live and die alongside their populace. It’s impossible for me to imagine New York as anything other than what it is right now, but it wasn’t always that way. It didn’t sprout out of the ground. People built it, and it changed with us. Lego Skylines gets that.

Once I got over the decision paralysis of, “Oh my God, look how big this is, what would I even do here?” I noticed that some folks really wanted more educational opportunities, so I built a university just outside of the city and a road to get people there. It wasn’t much, but I’d made the city better.

My demo ended shortly after that, but I walked away from it eager to come back and build a prettier (and more functional) pattern. The beauty of a city builder is you can do whatever you want, and Lego Skylines’ kinder, gentler approach – combined with the inherent appeal of building a city out of Legos – seems like it will scratch that itch. It might not be as cool as building Legos with your family on Christmas, but you can still make something beautiful if you try.

While you're here, check out these recent previews of other big upcoming games we've checked out recently!

Will Borger is an IGN freelancer. You can find him on Bluesky @edgarallanbro.

articles.title: Xbox app is coming to TCL TVs just as Microsoft rolls out pay-as-you-go cloud gaming
articles.summary: Xbox Cloud Gaming is coming to more TVs, just as Microsoft makes some major changes to its cloud gaming service.
articles.body: Microsoft is partnering with TCL to bring its Xbox app to supported TCL smart TVs. The Xbox app lets you connect to Xbox Cloud Gaming and stream Game Pass titles or select games you own as part of a subscription. The Xbox app will arrive on TCL TVs at some point “in the coming months,” which is just in time for Microsoft’s new pay-as-you-go option for Xbox Cloud Gaming in November. This will let anyone access the cloud streaming service without the need to subscribe to Xbox Game Pass — ideal for people who don’t own an Xbox console. Microsoft has also been testing free, ad-supported cloud gaming for Xbox Insiders, which could roll out soon and provide even more options to access Xbox Cloud Gaming. While Microsoft is opening up access to cloud gaming, it’s also limiting monthly cloud hours for Game Pass subscribers. Xbox Game Pass Ultimate subscribers will be limited to just 15 hours of cloud access a month, with 10 hours for Premium subscribers, and a measly 5 hours for Game Pass Essential. Game Pass subscribers will need to purchase bundles of cloud hours if they need additional playtime. TCL is the latest in a line of TV manufacturers to partner with Microsoft to rollout the Xbox app. Hisense started adding the Xbox app to its TVs running the VIDAA OS earlier this year, and many Samsung, LG, and Amazon Fire TV devices also have access to the Xbox app.

articles.title: Exodus Romance Options Are Not Gender-Locked for Both Male and Female Leads
articles.summary: The upcoming Mass Effect-style sci-fi RPG is giving players freedom with relationships and romance options regardless of the gender they choose for their protagonist.
articles.body:
As you'd expect from a space opera RPG that shares many similarties with Mass Effect, the upcoming Exodus from developer Archetype Entertainment has character relationships that you can build through dialogue choices, interactions, and decisions they make. This includes romance options; while you can choose to play as a male or female version of the lead character Jun Aslan, all character romance options will be available to you.

I spoke with Exodus narrative director (and former BioWare narrative lead) Drew Karpyshyn and asked him about how romance options work in this new game. "First of all, the player drives the romances and they are not gender-locked," he told me.

Karpyshyn continued explaining the depth of the system and how you can have multiple partners, saying, "There's no situation where a character is going to romance you if you didn't take the initiative. We want to put you in situations where you can potentially try to romance more than one character. Sometimes it'll go well, sometimes it won't depending on the character and depending on the choices you make. Like real life, it's complicated, right? We want it to be complicated."

It seems you won't be able to have everyone you want, however, and Exodus is said to pose tough decisions in both story moments and relationship dynamics. "We want to put you in positions where you can't make everybody happy. You're going to have to choose. Who do you side with, knowing that you will gain or lose affinity with one of these companions?" Karpyshyn said, before explaining that the choices you make throughout a playthrough will effect how characters perceive you. And rather than romance being a mechanical type of gameplay system, he mentioned, "We're leaning more toward the romances being a sort of role-playing relationship thing as opposed to being tied directly to gameplay."

With regard to any differences between the male and female versions of Jun, Karpyshyn said, "We really want players to feel like their choice of whether to play male or female is the choice that makes them happy... we're telling a story that works regardless, so there's not a lot of differences in how characters react to you."

The next logical question you'd probably ask is: what about sex scenes? Well, Exodus has them, too. “I think we're a bit closer to the reserved side, but certainly it's clear what's happening, but tasteful is a good way to describe it,” game director Chris King explained in a separate conversation with us at gamescom 2026.

With queer romance being a major feature in games such as Baldur's Gate 3 and even the older Mass Effect games, Exodus seems to be following suit. And we'll see how it plays out when Exodus launches on April 7, 2027 for PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X|S, and PC. Be sure to check out my hands-on impressions of Exodus and read my full interview with Drew Karpyshyn where we discuss how choices, consequences, and the morality system work.

Michael Higham is an editor at IGN who regularly contributes with reviews, previews, features, and news in written and video form. He's usually entrusted with covering long RPGs and tech products, but he's got range when it comes to games. You'll also catch him at events and hosting video content, including IGN's weekly podcast Unlocked .

articles.title: Onimusha Shows Why Capcom Is on a Winning Streak
articles.summary: Onimusha: Way of the Sword succeeds because it does what Capcom games like Resident Evil 7 and Monster Hunter: World did before it - combine the best of the series' past with the best of the wider industry to create a brilliant modern formula.
articles.body:
There are very few publishers who can claim to have had quite as prosperous a decade as Capcom. The company’s 10 best-selling games all launched within the past 10 years, a chain of good fortune that began with 2017’s Resident Evil 7. Capcom’s reimagining of gaming’s most important survival horror series became something of a formula for its wider success, and that template can be seen in action once again with this year’s Onimusha: Way of the Sword .

Aside from a couple of remasters and spin-off projects, Onimusha has lain dormant for 20 years. The entire original four-part series was released during the PS2 era, and so there have been nearly three whole console generations of progress since the last entry, 2006’s Dawn of Dreams . That project introduced what was, until Way of the Sword, Onimusha’s most “modern” idea: a fully 3D camera. For its earlier entries, Onimusha used fixed camera perspectives and pre-rendered backdrops, much like the original Resident Evils.

There's a good reason for that: Onimusha basically was Resident Evil. Set predominantly within the grounds of a single castle, 2001’s Onimusha: Warlords is a game of solving puzzles, unlocking doors, and eating herbs to stay alive. Shinji Mikami, co-creator of Resident Evil, even advised on the project. The series shed more of that survival horror blood with each successive entry, but when it comes to a brand new Onimusha for the 2020s, it would not have been surprising to see Capcom return to those roots and essentially clone its Resident Evil 2 remake but fill it with samurai and demons. Afterall, much of Resident Evil 7’s success is thanks to revitalising the past, the Baker Estate being a Southern Gothic variant of the Spencer Mansion.

But Onimusha: Way of the Sword is not Resident Evil with samurai. If anything, it’s Capcom’s answer to Sony Santa Monica Studio’s modern God of War games. It features furious melee combat with an array of flashy abilities. You face monstrous bosses, some of which repeat multiple times. Treasures are hidden behind knotty environmental puzzles. Your protagonist, Miyamoto Musashi, squeezes through gaps, and is accompanied by a disembodied advisor who is much too talkative.

This is still Capcom’s formula in action, though, just a different side of it. Resident Evil 7 ’s success is as much about wider influences as it is refocusing on roots. To put Resident Evil back on track after the much-too-bombastic RE6, Capcom studied the horror landscape. It saw the success of projects like Frictional Games’ utterly terrifying Amnesia: The Dark Descent, and how the limited vision enforced by a first-person perspective could create an oppressive atmosphere – an approach that turned the simple corridors of Hideo Kojima’s PT into a looping nightmare. Combined with the labyrinthine level design the company had perfected back in the 1990s, it would make for the ideal series reboot. Resident Evil 7 was born. A similar approach can be seen in Capcom's other landmark game of the decade – by adopting the open world format so popular in the West, Monster Hunter: World transformed a niche concern into Capcom’s best-selling game by over 10 million copies.

In Way of the Sword, you can see how Capcom has studied the success of God of War and similar modern action-adventure games in order to find a new identity for Onimusha. Those learnings are not just echoed in level design and individual features, but also in tone: Way of the Sword is surprisingly funny. Like Nathan Drake, Musashi adventures through Kyoto armed with a thousand one-liners. His face, modelled on legendary actor and Kurosawa collaborator, Toshiro Mifune, is incredibly expressive, often for comedic effect.

The original games were campy, but more so because that was simply the way games were written at the time – like the original Resident Evil, there’s a lot of unintentional comedy in Warlords’ script. But, as with the modern era of Resident Evil, Capcom made a deliberate choice. With Resi, it pushed aside the camp and doubled down on the horror. The remakes are much grimier than their parent games, while RE7 has the kind of filthy fears that’ll give you tetanus, and RE8 contains the series’ most terrifying scares in House Beneviento. For Onimusha, Capcom has pushed the other way, turning the Power Rangers camp of the original games into a deliberate flavour. While many will understandably opt for the Japanese VO for a more “authentic” experience, I think the bizarre Britishness of Way of the Sword’s English dub is intentional – not just in making Musashi more amusing, but turning his Genma adversaries into the Kyoto equivalent of London-accented orcs (a “Looks like samurai’s back on the menu, boys!” would fit in perfectly). While Way of the Sword does have its fair share of darkness and terror to reflect the survival horror leanings of the original games, there’s plenty to laugh at here, and Capcom wants you to chuckle.

But Capcom also wants you to sweat, and that’s where Way of the Sword’s greatest achievement comes in. As fun as the original games are, Onimusha has never offered any significant depth in its swordplay. If it were to live up to its new subtitle, the latest entry absolutely needed a new approach. It took that approach from FromSoftware’s masterpiece, Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice , and it smartly did so without turning Onimusha into a soulslike.

There’s already some debate as to how Souls-y Way of the Sword is, and for the most part the answer is “not at all.” But when it comes to Onimusha’s bosses, the Sekiro similarity is undeniable. The parry is your greatest weapon, and matching the rhythmic patterns of your enemy’s blade is the primary way of opening up attack windows. Like Sekiro, this is a game of wearing down an enemy’s stamina before inflicting massive bursts of damage, and then resetting the deadly dance to do it all over again. A delicate balance of offence and defence is demanded, as giving your enemy space allows them to regain stamina, the very thing you need to erode away to inflict the most severe punishment. You can’t simply spam attacks to burn through the enemy’s healthbar, or chug consumables to allow a barrage of your flashiest damage dealers – you must fight using a very precise set of tools, picked in response to a very particular set of attack patterns. Alongside limited heals, multi-phase fights, and the combat’s frenetic flow, it’s hard to deny that Onimusha’s new approach to bosses isn’t following in FromSoftware’s shinobi footsteps.

But Capcom wouldn’t have enjoyed its decade of success if it just pilfered from popular games with little care for how those ideas were implemented. Again, Way of the Sword is not a soulslike, and you can see that in its wider design. Genre rules like bonfires, world resets, and loss of XP resources are absent. Regular enemies are, if anything, too easy. And there’s not a poison swamp in sight. While all this does contribute to the feeling of the bosses being substantial difficulty spikes along the campaign’s route, it also ensures that Onimusha is not a grueling experience in the way that FromSoftware’s games can be – even when you’re on your sixth attempt at a boss, there’s no infuriating run-back to contend with, and that goes a long way to ensuring you don’t lose your patience when faced with a particularly tricky roadblock.

It’s this elegant adaptation of ideas from beyond Capcom’s walls that ensured both Monster Hunter and Resident Evil became the modern juggernauts they are. While MH: World expanded its literal horizons to allow for a more expansive environment, it was careful not to take on the bloat of contemporary open world games. It was still focused on the hunt. Resident Evil 7 may have adopted the perspective of Amnesia, PT, and Alien: Isolation, but it rejected their combatless approaches and put a gun in your hand – exactly as Resident Evil should be. In all these examples, it’s clear that Capcom understands both each trend’s mass appeal and how to reinterpret that trend in a way that’s appropriate to the IP in question.

While it remains to be seen if Capcom’s resurrection of its long-dormant samurai game will be quite as financially successful as its Resident Evil and Monster Hunter revitalisations, it’s clear that the Capcom formula has worked beautifully for Onimusha: Way of the Sword. It has launched to near-universal critical adoration , and its impressive pre-release demo quickly earned it a legion of eager fans. With any luck, Onimusha is back, and its next game will feature whatever the swordplay equivalent to House Beneviento is.

Matt Purslow is IGN's Executive Editor of Features.

articles.title: Harry Potter Series' Dobby and Young Voldemort Casting Revealed
articles.summary: HBO has revealed a trio of key roles for the second season of its lavish Harry Potter series: Dobby, Ginny Weasley and Tom Riddle, better known as a young Lord Voldemort.
articles.body:
HBO has revealed a trio of key roles for the second season of its lavish Harry Potter series: Dobby, Ginny Weasley and Tom Riddle, better known as a young Lord Voldemort.

17-year-old British actor, presenter and comedian Lenny Rush will star as Dobby the House-elf, who is introduced in Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets and goes on to play a memorable role later in the series. Rush previously starred in British children's TV series The Dumping Ground, though has also starred in episodes of Doctor Who, as well as Taskmaster.

Tom Riddle, meanwhile, will be played by 18-year-old Billy Barratt. While not yet a household name, Barratt is currently filming the Amazon Prime adaptation of hit narrative video game Life is Strange, and also playing an antagonist (Nathan Prescott) in that. If you watched Kraven the Hunter, you'll also have seen him pop up as a young Dmitri Smerdyakov.

Lastly, HBO has now confirmed that newcomer Bonnie Hill will portray Ginny Weasley from the series' second season onwards. The character's previous actress dropped out of appearing in future episodes following the show's first season.

Production on the series' second run is now underway, as HBO attempts to leave as small a gap between seasons as possible. Still, bosses have admitted that the show will not air annually, meaning that episodes shot this year will likely not arrive until 2028.

Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone TV Show Character Images

Actors returning for the series' second season, which adapts Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets, include Dominic McLaughlin as Harry Potter, Arabella Stanton as Hermione Granger, Alastair Stout as Ron Weasley, John Lithgow as Albus Dumbledore, Paapa Essiedu as Severus Snape, and Nick Frost as Rubeus Hagrid.

Last month, it was revealed that Game of Thrones star Kit Harington will portray Gilderoy Lockhart — a role previously given to Superman star Nicholas Hoult, who later dropped out due to scheduling issues.

HBO will air the series' first season beginning this Christmas, with episodes then continuing into early 2027.

Tom Phillips is IGN's News Editor. You can reach Tom at tom_phillips@ign.com or find him on Bluesky @tomphillipseg.bsky.social

articles.title: 30 Open World Masterpieces You Need to Play - IGN30 - IGN
articles.summary: Open-world games. Arguably, no other genre has defined modern gaming more than the expansive, experimental, and exciting places this genre has taken us to. Over the past 30 years, we’ve gone from grey, empty streets begging to be torn up in a blocky muscle car to glorious, colourful fantasy lands full of adventure and opportunity. But what are the games that have stood out the most, pushed the form forward, and ultimately led to GTA 6’s moment? As part of IGN 30, I’m going to try to answer that question by walking you through five distinct flavours of open-world game before deciding on the greatest of them all. From web-swinging superheroes and sword-swinging monster hunters to bank heists and shrine raids, here are the 30 masterpieces of open-world game design.

articles.title: Game of Thrones Stage Play The Mad King Is Coming to London in 2027
articles.summary: Following a sold-out run at the Royal Shakespeare Company, George R.R. Martin’s Game of Thrones: The Mad King stage play will move to London in 2027.
articles.body:
Game of Thrones: The Mad King is coming to London next year.

Author George R.R. Martin has revealed that the Royal Shakespeare Company will bring the prequel stage play to the UK capital in 2027. A venue or premiere date has not been announced yet.

“I had a splendid time in Stratford upon Avon for the premier of Duncan Macmillan and Dominic Cooke’s epic new stage production of Game of Thrones: The Mad King. And furthermore I’m thrilled to announce that the production will be moving on to London to share the experience with a wider audience,” Martin wrote on his blog .

Game of Thrones: The Mad King began its six-week run in July at the Royal Shakespeare Theatre in Stratford. It closes this week, having earned rave reviews and many sold out shows.

The play is set roughly 15 years before Martin’s first A Song of Ice and Fire book begins. It chronicles the downfall of King Aerys II Targaryen, aka “The Mad King” who was overthrown during Robert’s Rebellion.

IGN writer Helen O’Hara caught one of the productions during its run at Stratford and broke down 9 things the play reveals about Westeros that Game of Thrones fans would want to know , including how Rhaegar Targaryen was deeply wronged by history and that Daenerys and Jon Snow were conceived on the same night.
